questions.question: What does scalar multiplication k·P mean on an elliptic curve group?
options: Add the point P to itself k times using the group law
Multiply the coordinates (x, y) of P by k in the integers
Raise the x-coordinate of P to the power k modulo p
Compute a new curve parameter set by scaling a and b by k
questions.explanation: Scalar multiplication is repeated group addition. Coordinate-wise integer multiplication is not the group operation.

questions.question: In the standard double-and-add algorithm (left-to-right), what happens for each processed scalar bit?
options: Always double the accumulator, and conditionally add P when the bit is 1
Always add P, and conditionally double only when the bit is 1
Always invert in the field, and conditionally negate when the bit is 0
Always multiply x by 2, and conditionally divide y by 2 in F_p
questions.explanation: Double-and-add performs one doubling per bit and an extra addition only for 1 bits.

questions.question: What key property of the non-adjacent form (NAF) helps reduce point additions compared to plain binary?
options: NAF has no adjacent nonzero digits, making the representation sparser
NAF forces every digit to be 1, so additions can be merged together
NAF guarantees the scalar has exactly half as many bits as binary
NAF replaces doubling with squaring, which is faster in every field
questions.explanation: NAF recoding avoids consecutive nonzero digits, which lowers the expected number of additions.

questions.question: Which digit set is used by classic NAF recoding?
options: Digits are chosen from {−1, 0, +1}
Digits are chosen from {0, 1, 2, 3}
Digits are chosen from {−2, −1, +1, +2}
Digits are chosen from {0, 1} only
questions.explanation: Classic NAF uses signed digits −1, 0, +1, allowing subtraction via adding −P.

questions.question: For wNAF with window size w, what values are typically precomputed for a point P?
options: Odd multiples P, 3P, 5P, ..., (2^{w-1}−1)P
All multiples P, 2P, 3P, ..., (2^w−1)P
Only powers of two P, 2P, 4P, ..., 2^{w-1}P
Only even multiples 2P, 4P, 6P, ..., (2^w−2)P
questions.explanation: wNAF digits are odd and bounded, so a small table of odd multiples supports fast lookups.

questions.question: What does simple power analysis (SPA) exploit in a naive double-and-add implementation?
options: A detectable difference between “double-only” and “double+add” steps reveals scalar bits
A proof that scalar multiplication is impossible without factoring the field modulus
A weakness where doubling fails unless the point is a generator of the full curve
A method to compute discrete logs by solving one modular equation from an observed trace
questions.explanation: If an attacker can tell whether an addition occurred for a bit, the scalar’s bit pattern leaks.

questions.question: Why do real implementations often avoid affine formulas inside scalar multiplication loops?
options: Affine formulas require field inversions, so projective coordinates reduce expensive inversions
Affine formulas cannot represent the identity element, so they are mathematically invalid
Affine formulas always leak the scalar, while projective formulas are always constant-time
Affine formulas only work for curves with a = 0, so they fail on most named curves
questions.explanation: Affine point addition/doubling typically needs an inversion per operation; projective systems trade inversions for cheaper multiplications.

questions.question: How should a correct scalar multiplication routine handle a negative scalar k < 0?
options: Replace k by −k and replace P by −P, then multiply as usual
Replace k by −k and then negate only the x-coordinate of the output
Reduce k modulo the field prime p and compute the result with that value
Return the identity element because negative scalars are not defined
questions.explanation: In an abelian group, (−k)·(−P) equals k·P. Negating only one coordinate is not a valid point negation.
